title: Token Boundary Coalescer and Grace Periods: heuristics for early-ack and eviction
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a lightweight component — the Token Boundary Coalescer (TBC) — plus an associated set of grace-period heuristics that together reduce wasted work and noisy partial-token emissions in our streaming generation path. The goal: preserve millisecond-level responsiveness for tail latency while avoiding too-frequent flushes and kernel thrash that increase GPU occupancy and cost.

Motivation and observed issues:
- Production telemetry shows a bimodal distribution of streaming flush intervals: a large number of micro-flushes (<5ms apart) caused by rapid application-level cancellations or tiny model increments, and a smaller set of 30–200ms flushes that align to natural token boundaries. Micro-flushes inflate kernel invocation counts and increase KV cache churn.
- Partial-token emissions (partial UTF-8 sequences, mid-subword pieces) are user-visible in some clients and lead to awkward UI flicker. Clients that prematurely ACK partial tokens create ordering and deduplication complexity for downstream tracing.
- Cancellation races: when a request is cancelled, we sometimes emit a short partial chunk before the cancellation is handled, which then triggers redundant fallback work in the gateway.

Design overview:
- Token Boundary Coalescer (TBC): a small, per-request state machine sitting between the runtime emission layer and the network layer. It coalesces micro-emissions into semantically complete token boundaries using light-weight heuristics (see heuristics section). The TBC is intentionally separate from the kernel scheduler so it can be tuned without touching kernel logic.
- Grace periods: per-request, bounded timers (configurable by route) that allow the TBC to wait a short window for additional bytes before flushing. Two timers: soft-grace (short, default 8–12ms) and hard-grace (longer, default 60–120ms) to handle variance.
- Early-ack policy: network-level ACKs are decoupled from flush-to-client. We introduce an intermediate ACK state (ack_prelim) for micro-chunks which signals receipt without exposing content to the client UI until a token boundary is reached. This reduces duplicate client-side reconnection/fallback.

Heuristics for coalescing (ordered by priority):
1) UTF-8 safe boundary: never release a chunk that ends with an incomplete multi-byte UTF-8 sequence.
2) Subword boundary detection: prefer to wait until the BPE/subword model indicates end-of-piece markers (model can expose a byte-level boundary flag in the emission metadata).
3) Entropy threshold: if the last N bytes have high byte entropy consistent with non-text tokens (e.g., binary embeddings or compressed payload), flush immediately to avoid stalls.
4) Latency budget: if the request latency budget (route-level SLO) is near exhaustion, bypass coalescing and flush immediately.
5) Cancellation window: if a cancellation is observed within soft-grace, hold the flush until the kernel confirms no more tokens were queued (race mitigation). If cancellation observed after hard-grace, flush and then cancel.

KV cache and eviction semantics:
- Coalescer-aware cache pinning: when the TBC holds back emission, the KV cache must retain pinned KV slices for the duration of the soft-grace plus a small safety margin (default 6ms) to avoid recomputation if the coalescer decides to concat an incoming fragment. Implement as a pin token issued by the TBC to the cache manager.
- Eviction timeline: typical KV eviction windows are extended by soft-grace + hard-grace while a request is active. This is conservative but avoids recompute: KV TTL extension = max(request_active_time_remaining, soft_grace + 2ms).

Interaction with scheduler and kernels:
- Kernel invocation batching: TBC delays should be visible to the scheduler as a 'linger' hint so the scheduler can opportunistically batch subsequent small kernel calls into a larger kernel invocation. The scheduler should expose a small window (configurable) where it will combine micro-invocations unless a high-priority request is pending.
- Preemption policy: if a kernel preemption is needed for an urgent request, TBC must be able to flush immediately (bypass both grace timers) to prevent head-of-line blocking for SLO-critical traffic.

Cancellation and idempotency:
- Idempotent output tokens: every emitted token/chunk must carry a monotonically increasing emission sequence id (per-request). Clients and gateways use this id to deduplicate replays after reconnects.
- Cancellation handshake: when a cancellation signal arrives, the runtime signals TBC with a cancel-intent. TBC will: (a) cancel any outstanding soft-grace timers, (b) flush only if the last buffered bytes complete a token boundary within a short fast-path (<=2ms), otherwise drop the buffer and emit a cancellation marker to the network layer. This reduces mid-token partials on cancel.

Client-visible guarantees and fallback behavior:
- Visible-only-on-boundary: default behavior is that clients only see emitted chunks that end on safe token boundaries (UTF-8 + subword). Configurable per-route for low-latency modes where partials are acceptable.
- Fallback logic for streaming clients: if the client opts into low-latency partials, they receive partial-byte updates with explicit partial flags; otherwise, the client only receives full-boundary updates and will see slightly higher perceived latency but much cleaner UI.

Metrics and instrumentation:
- New metrics: tbc.coalesced_flush_ratio, tbc.soft_grace_missed_count, tbc.hard_grace_escapes, tbc.cancel_flushed_vs_dropped, tbc.pin_hold_time_ms.
- Dashboards: per-route breakdown of coalesced vs immediate flushes, kernel invocation counts pre/post TBC rollout, KV-recompute rate.

Experiment plan and rollout:
1) Canary: implement TBC behind a feature flag on a small set of low-risk routes (internal chatbots). Measure coalesced_flush_ratio and kernel invocation drop.
2) Beta: enable soft-grace only on 25% of routes; add pin token and KV TTL extension. Monitor KV recompute and cost.
3) Gradual rollout: once coalescing shows >=15% reduction in kernel invocations and <2% user-visible latency regression, expand to all hosted API text-generation routes with a configurable route parameter.

Backward compatibility and API changes:
- No change to generation API surface by default. Expose route-level options: streaming.coalesce_mode = {"none", "utf8_safe", "full_subword"}, streaming.soft_grace_ms, streaming.hard_grace_ms.
- Telemetry additions are read-only and will not affect existing dashboards.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Optimal default soft_grace: our lab tests suggest 8–12ms hits the sweet spot, but client network jitter at mobile endpoints could change this. We may need an adaptive soft_grace per-client-class.
- Where to place subword-boundary flags: best if emitted by model kernels, but this requires a minor kernel API addition and coordination with model-onboarding. Alternative: heuristics on whitespace/punctuation risk misfires for agglutinative languages.
- Memory cost of per-request pin tokens at high concurrency: need stress testing to ensure pins do not cause KV memory pressure.

Implementation notes / prototype checklist:
- Add TBC component in emission pipeline (runtime/emission/tbc.*). Keep it stateless across requests except for short-lived timers and pin token id.
- Add pin token API surface to cache manager: Cache.Pin(token_id, kv_keys, hold_ms). Simple reference count semantics.
- Kernel change (optional): add boundary_flag in token emission metadata. Fallback to BPE heuristics when absent.
- Add metrics and tracing spans: tbc.wait_ms, tbc.flush_reason, tbc.cancel_decision.

Backward compatibility experiment idea:
- A/B test mode where TBC only merges emissions that the client explicitly requests via a header (X-Redwood-Coalesce: aggressive). This gives app teams a fast migration path.

Appendix: short pseudo-flow
1) runtime emits chunk -> TBC records bytes + seq_id -> check heuristics (UTF8 safe? subword flag?) -> if boundary -> flush immediately; else start soft_grace timer -> if new bytes arrive within soft_grace and make boundary -> flush; else on soft_grace expiry start hard_grace and optionally flush if latency budget low -> if hard_grace expiry -> force flush with best-effort boundary trimming.

Notes and related links:
- See related Linear ticket R-2214 and runtime PR 482 for an initial PoC. Slack thread #streaming-coalesce has early UX reports.

Open tasks:
- Prototype TBC and run load test at 1000 rps synthetic with mixed token lengths.
- Implement pin token GC and safety margin to avoid leaks.
- Decide on default route-level config and document in hosted-api runbooks.

Authors: Maya Chen (primary), with contributions from Luca Perez and Anika Rao.
